t: Minimum Threshold Path With Limited Heavy Edges
o: We must pick an integer threshold T so that every edge with weight <= T is 'light' and the rest are 'heavy', then find a path from source to target using at most k heavy edges, minimizing T. Feasibility is monotone: if some T works, any larger T also works (edges only get lighter), which immediately suggests binary search over candidate thresholds. For a fixed T, we need the minimum possible number of heavy edges on any source-target path; if that minimum is <= k, T is feasible. Example 1: with T=4 the path 0->1->4->3 uses exactly one heavy edge ([0,1,5]), and no smaller T keeps that path valid within k=1. Example 2 has no connectivity between source and target at all, so -1 regardless of k. Constraints (n, m <= 10^3) allow roughly O(m^2 log m) work, so binary search plus an O(n+m) shortest-path-by-count per check fits comfortably.
k: Feasibility is monotone in the threshold: raising T can only turn heavy edges into light ones, so binary search over sorted distinct weights (plus 0) finds the answer.
For a fixed threshold, the minimum number of heavy edges on any path is computable with a 0-1 BFS / Dijkstra where light edges cost 0 and heavy edges cost 1.
If source == target the answer is 0; if target is unreachable even with all edges light, return -1.

a.n: Approach 1: Linear scan over all candidate thresholds
a.i: Try every candidate threshold in increasing order (0 and each distinct edge weight). For each, run a 0-1 BFS computing dist[v] = minimum number of heavy edges from source to v; if dist[target] <= k we found the smallest feasible threshold. This is the most direct translation of the problem statement and clearly correct because feasibility is monotone.
s: Collect candidates {0} ∪ {all edge weights}, sorted ascending.
For each candidate T, build adjacency marking each edge as cost 0 (w <= T) or cost 1.
Run 0-1 BFS (deque) from source to get min heavy-edge counts.
a.t: O(m^2) — up to m+1 candidate thresholds, each checked with an O(n+m) 0-1 BFS; fine for n, m <= 1000.
a.sp: O(n + m) — adjacency list, distance array, and deque.

a.n: Approach 2: Binary search on the threshold
a.i: Since feasibility is monotone in T, instead of scanning all candidates linearly we binary search over the sorted array of distinct weights prefixed with 0. Each probe runs the same O(n+m) 0-1 BFS feasibility check. This cuts the number of checks from O(m) to O(log m).
s: Build sorted candidate list C = [0] + sorted distinct weights.
Binary search for the leftmost index i such that feasible(C[i]).
feasible(T): 0-1 BFS from source with light/heavy costs; true iff dist[target] <= k.
If even C[last] is infeasible, return -1.
a.t: O((n + m) log m) — binary search does O(log m) probes, each an O(n + m) 0-1 BFS.
a.sp: O(n + m) — adjacency list, distances, and deque.

w: In an interview, lead with the monotonicity observation and propose binary search over thresholds (Approach 2); mention the linear scan as a stepping stone. Pitfalls: forgetting the candidate 0 (needed when source equals target or all path edges are already <= 0-weight cases — here weights >= 1, but source==target still requires returning 0); returning -1 only after proving infeasibility at the largest candidate; using plain BFS without the 0-1 deque trick would give wrong heavy counts unless you use Dijkstra on unit costs. Edge cases: disconnected graph (-1), source == target (0), k = 0 (path must use only light edges), duplicate edges and self-loops (handled naturally). Follow-ups: solve for many (source, target, k) queries offline (sort queries, add edges incrementally with small-to-large merging of component-level 'min heavy budget' structures), or handle dynamic edge insertions.
